claim: ACH did not improve the accuracy of human analysts' probability judgments against a Bayesian benchmark; point estimates in two labs favour the control (MAE .26 vs .21, N=50; no difference N=227, N=147).
schema_part: S5/none: do not add a full matrix step
agent_test: Equal-token A/B: plain answer vs ACH-matrix prompt on hypothesis-ranking items with known posteriors; compare MAE to Bayes.
audit_note: All three experiments come from one research program (Mandel is an author of all; Karvetski of two of them, with the third by Mandel, Karvetski and Dhami), so 'two labs' is wrong, and the N=147 study found ACH decreased coherence, not 'no difference'; MAE .26 vs .21 (N=50, p=.14) and N=227 no advantage are correct.

claim: ACH made analysts use base rates less (12% vs 52%, Dhami 2019) and trained analysts weight non-diagnostic evidence about 30% as much as diagnostic (Karvetski and Mandel 2020).
agent_test: Plant non-diagnostic and base-rate cues; measure whether a matrix prompt shifts weight to them more than plain prompting.
audit_note: Dhami 2019 (12% vs 52% using base rates, n=25 per group, p=.002) and Karvetski and Mandel 2020 (non-diagnostic evidence weight about 32% / 30%) both come from Mandel's group; also the Karvetski and Mandel participants were 227 graduates, not trained analysts.

claim: ACH improves recognition of which cues are diagnostic (usefulness rating correlates .68 with true gain vs .17 in control) and lists more cues (92% vs 68%) without improving the final judgments.
agent_test: Compare cue-usefulness ratings of the agent with and without a diagnosticity step, and then final accuracy.

claim: ACH users often deviate from the rules: 20 of 25 used consistent evidence; only 1 of 25 applied the scoring rule consistently; 64% final conclusions matched their own matrix.
agent_test: Check whether the agent's final answer follows its own matrix; a gap means the matrix is decoration.

claim: In Mandel et al. 2018 both ACH and control probabilities summed above 1 (1.77 vs 1.54), a difference that was not significant (p=.13), while a separate 147-person study from the same group found ACH decreased coherence; coherentizing cut mean absolute error from .23 to .15 and averaging all 50 coherentized judgments gave .09. For LLMs (2026), judgments elicited in one dialogue violated probability rules far less than across separate chats (10% of scenarios for Gemini-2.5-Pro, 1 of 30 for Gemma), eliciting a full panel of 14 related events in one query brought incoherence near the rounding floor, and for GPT-OSS-120B averaging up to 5 samples helped only modestly because 95% of answers were identical.
agent_test: At equal tokens: plain vs plain+coherentize vs ACH+coherentize on multi-hypothesis probability items.
audit_note: ACH-vs-control coherence difference was not significant in the 50-analyst study (sum 1.77 vs 1.54, p=.13); it was significant only in the separate 147-person study from the same group; the 5-sample averaging result was measured on GPT-OSS-120B only. MAE .23 to .15 and pool .09 verified.
claim_before_audit: ACH gives more incoherent (non-additive, sums above 1) probabilities than control, but coherentization plus aggregation recovers most error (MAE .23 to .15; pool of 50 .09). The repair, not the ACH step, helps. LLM note (2026): one joint elicitation of all related events, or a visible running belief state in one dialogue, removes most LLM incoherence; averaging 5 same-model samples helps little (95% of answers identical).

claim: Presenting evidence as a matrix with hypotheses in rows reduces confirmation-only choices versus text (Dhami 2024: chi2(2)=9.43, p=.009), but a classic ACH-style columns layout did not (p=.327). Layout, not the method, matters; sample was young students.
agent_test: Vary layout of evidence in the prompt (rows vs columns vs prose) and count confirm-only choices.

claim: Evidence that ACH reduces confirmation bias is thin: positive only for non-analysts in Lehner 2008 (N=24); null for analysts, Whitesmith (8/39 biased after training) and Maegherman (N=191, 38% compliance).
agent_test: Measure agent order effects of evidence with and without ACH prompt; compare confirmation index.

claim: In field data (n=138 reports) use of ACH correlated slightly negatively with accuracy (r=-.08), while timelines (.28) and Bayes (.22) were positive; low power and confounded.
agent_test: Not directly testable; use as weak prior.

claim: A critical review of six ACH experiments (Wilcox and Mandel) found no accuracy benefit and some harm, and no randomized test shows ACH improves accuracy; Heuer (1999) asserts that ACH 'increases the odds of getting the right answer' without citing a test, and per Mandel and Tetlock (2018) Heuer replied in 2010 that if testing did not replicate exactly how ACH is used in the Intelligence Community he would be inclined to ignore it and stick with common sense.
agent_test: None needed; policy claim.
audit_note: Heuer's quoted 2010 reply (via Mandel and Tetlock) was conditional: he would ignore testing that does not replicate how ACH is used in the Intelligence Community, not tests that failed; the two review sources share an author (Mandel). Heuer's 'increases the odds of getting the right answer' and 'proven process' are confirmed untested.
claim_before_audit: No peer-reviewed randomized test shows ACH improves accuracy; the claim 'increases the odds' is asserted in Heuer 1999 without a test, and Heuer said he would ignore failed tests.

claim: In LLMs, a zero-shot ACH-style prompt gives small multi-agent gains (+2.0 to +2.3 all-average, MMLU-family) over unstructured deciders (about 0); large gains come from training, not the ACH prompt.
agent_test: Replicate on our tasks with a single agent at equal tokens: ACH decider vs plain decider.

claim: In PRISM (MuSR murders, 10 LLMs) the ACH matrix stage added only +0.8 points (11% of the structuring gain); evidence filtering and multi-view profiling gave +5.7 and +6.7 of +13.2 in total. CoT did not help (57.2 vs 58.1). The +0.8 is one deterministic run on 250 items per model with no interval; my rough SE is about 1.3 points, so it is indistinguishable from zero.
agent_test: Ablate matrix on a murder-mystery set at equal tokens; compare self-consistency (+5.1 here).

claim: HypoArena: an agent mode with 12 analytic skills including ACH moved arena rating from +88 to about -60 across 15 models, uncorrelated with baseline strength (rho -0.10); ACH alone was not ablated. Re-read: no per-skill ablation, no skill-usage counts, no token cost; failure mode is candidate compression (qualitative).
agent_test: Run per-skill ablation for ACH on our own hypothesis-generation items.

claim: Investigation-style scaffolds with competing explanations help LLMs: SIA 79.2 vs direct 67.3 vs 'think of competing explanations' 67.5; but gain comes from the full pipeline (removing structured investigation costs 6.4), not from listing alternatives alone.
agent_test: Compare listing alternatives vs full investigate-critique-adjudicate loop at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs are confirmation-biased in hypothesis testing: success correlates positively with disconfirming tests (11 settings), and cheap prompts like Think-in-Opposites help in all 11, while Dual-Goal hurt non-thinking models. Gains were statistically significant for thinking models only; thinking models spend about 1,000-2,300 tokens per turn; never compared with full ACH.
agent_test: Add a one-line disconfirm-first rule to the agent and measure I:C ratio and success.
audit_note: Gains significant for thinking models only, TiO better in all 11, Dual-Goal small drop for non-thinking: all match Jhaveri et al.; the 1,000-2,300 tokens per turn figure and 'never compared with full ACH' were not directly checked.

claim: Task structure of hypothesis testing for LLMs: forcing disconfirmation benefits depend on model type (thinking vs non-thinking), so a fixed ACH protocol is not uniformly safe.
agent_test: Test each guardrail on both a reasoning and a non-reasoning model.

claim: Chatbot ACH tools and agent designs (ACH-Grounding, EMR-ACH, Roberts, Evron, Coulthart 2023) have no measured benefit; EMR-ACH pilot (N=79) is a majority-class baseline problem.
agent_test: Treat as untested.

claim: Wilcox and Mandel (2023) argue on theory grounds that ACH tells analysts to ignore consistent (confirming) evidence, including base rates, and their review lists as an empirical harm that ACH users double counted perfectly correlated cues, more so when the correlation was made salient (Karvetski, Mandel and Irwin 2020, same research group).
agent_test: Test agent double counting with correlated cue pairs, with and without matrix.
audit_note: Wilcox and Mandel's theory critique covers ignoring confirming evidence (including base rates) and Popper, but double counting of correlated cues is an empirical finding of Karvetski, Mandel and Irwin (same group) that the review only lists among harms, not a theory-level flaw they identify; the 0.14 vs 0.27 cue-distance figure is from the Karvetski preprint.
claim_before_audit: Wilcox and Mandel 2023 identify theory-level flaws: ACH ignores confirming evidence, and non-independence of cues is not handled (double counting increased under high salience).

claim: For current reasoning LLMs, heavy structure around belief updating no longer beats a plain in-context prompt (BED-LLM harness vs naive prompt on 20 Questions), and thinking mode alone fixes most Bayes errors on independent evidence (>=30% success loss without reasoning).
agent_test: Re-test each scaffold step on a thinking and a non-thinking model; drop the step if the plain prompt ties.

claim: Same-model repeated samples are correlated, not independent: wrong majority votes collapse on one wrong answer, CoT keeps the first wrong answer, and a same-model panel loses 4.7 to 34.6 points against a heterogeneous panel. More samples from one model are the LLM form of double counting.
agent_test: Plant duplicate or correlated cues and check whether weight rises; compare K same-model samples with K varied prompts at equal tokens.

claim: Public preprints (to 2026-11-03) contain no test of an ACH matrix prompt against a plain prompt on one model at equal tokens, no diagnosticity-only arm, no double-counting test of ACH, and no ACH-as-anchoring-debiaser test. These are open questions, not negative findings.
agent_test: Run the equal-token plain vs matrix vs diagnosticity-only comparison on Mandel-style items with known posteriors.

claim: Asking LLMs for related probabilities in separate chats gives frequent Dutch-book violations (over 50% of 30 scenarios for most model-axiom pairs); within one dialogue violations fall to 10% or one scenario of 30. Coherence varies about 100x between 15 models while Brier varies little.
agent_test: Keep one joint belief table in context; run a complement-question consistency check.
